sections.title: Methodological Foundations and Data Sources
sections.text: To understand developer behavior, researchers have increasingly focused on leveraging useful content from diverse sources, including Git, CVS, archived communications, online forums, and Community Question Answer (CQA) sites [3]. Prior software engineering research has empirically explored GitHub functionality to influence developer behavior and software engineering practices [4]. Additionally, software engineering researchers have explored using GitHub processes to recommend specific developer behaviors [4]. Studying developer activities related to various development tasks from these various sources can guide the development of tools that help developers find desired information more easily [3]. In specific analyses such as Magnet and Sticky, both commit actions and pull requests are viewed as developmental activity [1]. However, data collection presents challenges; some commits in the GitHub dataset do not contain the logins of their developers, instead only having the name and email obtained from the developer's local Git settings [2]. To address this, surrogate logins are created for developers of commits without GitHub logins by concatenating their local Git names and emails [2]. Furthermore, because most accepted pull requests sent from fork repositories are absent in the histories of original repositories, developer information must be mined from both the original and fork repositories [1].

sections.title: Automated Optimization and Prompt Engineering
sections.text: Researchers have developed various LLM-driven methods to automate the optimization of prompts, including OPRO, PromptAgent, EvoPrompt, RLPrompt, DSP, ProTeGi, PE2, and PREFER. Prompt engineering is defined as the process of crafting effective instructions to guide an LLM in generating desired outputs [2]. However, current prompt engineering techniques in SQL generation commonly fail to adapt well to changing data distributions or complex query requirements [3]. To mitigate issues such as hallucination, which conversational AI agents are prone to, the literature identifies prompt engineering and fine-tuning as the two most effective approaches [2]. Fine-tuning involves a structured seven-stage pipeline covering data preparation, model initialization, hyperparameter tuning, and deployment, utilizing parameter-efficient methods like LoRA and Half Fine-Tuning, though it faces challenges in managing imbalanced datasets. In specific domains, such as healthcare, emotion-aware LLMs (EA-LLMs) instructed by prompt engineering techniques are expected to emerge as communication channels between doctors and patients [1].

sections.text: To address user difficulties in constructing effective prompts, iteratively refining AI-generated responses, and assessing response reliability in unfamiliar domains, the "From Prompting to Partnering" study designed a prototype featuring Reflective Prompting, Section Regeneration, Input-Output Mapping, and Confidence indicators. DirectGPT offers a direct manipulation interface on top of ChatGPT that transforms direct manipulation actions into engineered prompts, resulting in participants being 50% faster and relying on 50% fewer and 72% shorter prompts. In the context of text summarization, researchers have mapped the design space of human-AI interaction to develop digital tools that support people in writing summaries. Abscribe introduces AI Modifiers, which are buttons created from prompts, auto-labeled by an LLM, reusable across passages, and editable over time. This button-based approach contrasts with free-form conversational UIs, which lead users to adopt a polite and verbose style rather than direct actions. Interactive methods, such as those used in MISP and DialSQL, employ a mixed-initiative approach by asking follow-up questions to clarify user intent, helping to establish "common ground" between the user and the AI [4]. sections.title: Defining Behavioral Evaluation
sections.text: Behavioral evaluation extends beyond aggregate metrics like accuracy or F1 score to examine model output patterns across input subgroups or slices [1]. This approach focuses on defining and testing the capabilities of an ML system against a specification of expected behaviors [1]. The method is closely related to subgroup or slice-based analysis, which calculates metrics on specific subsets of a dataset. For instance, facial classification models have been shown to perform significantly worse for darker-skinned women compared to lighter-skinned individuals, highlighting the need for such granular analysis [1]. However, many existing behavioral evaluation tools, including fairness toolkits, often fail to support the specific types of models, data, and behaviors that practitioners encounter in real-world scenarios [1].

sections.title: Zeno: A General-Purpose Framework
sections.text: To address the limitations of existing tools, Zeno was designed to reduce the learning curve and encourage the reuse of analyses by allowing users to perform behavioral evaluations on most ML tasks within a single framework [1]. The design of Zeno was informed by formative interviews with 18 ML practitioners, from which four main design goals were derived, including the support for comparison over time and no-code analysis [1]. Zeno builds upon prior work in visual analytics and testing. For example, FairVis is a visual analytics system that allows users to compare subs, while Errudite is a similar system for NLP models that enables users to create specific tests. Additionally, Zeno incorporates concepts from software engineering, such as metamorphic testing, which involves perturbing inputs to check for consistent outputs. Checklist is a metamorphic testing tool for NLP models that perturbs text to evaluate robustness. User feedback on Zeno indicated a desire for a direct way to add new instances and more interactive transformations, such as a slider to reduce amplitude, to facilitate testing with custom inputs [1]. Participants also suggested automatically generating ZENO API functions and configuration files for common ML libraries to streamline integration. To make the tool more accessible, technical terms such as 'metadata' were identified as potentially too niche for everyday users and could be renamed [1]. Future work suggests that longer-term, in-situ studies would provide more nuanced feedback regarding the utility of ZENO's model comparison features.

sections.title: Accelerating Annotation with Pretrained Models
sections.text: Several interfaces have been developed to accelerate annotation efforts by leveraging computational assistance. The sciverse_docspiral system leverages pretrained models for initial annotation, which significantly reduces the manual labeling workload compared to existing tools like COCO Annotator [3]. The data generated through this process is then used to train or fine-tune Progressive Models that better meet user requirements [3]. Similarly, TissueWand is a rapid histopathology annotation tool intended for the early stages of dataset curation, where no task-specific ML model yet exists to aid the effort [2][2]. This tool shows promise in replacing manual methods during these initial phases [2]. Another approach involves a CT-scan annotation tool for semantic segmentation that assists radiologists in labeling CT scans; this tool was evaluated by 6 radiologists. Cooperative Machine Learning (CML) techniques also aim to reduce manual labelling efforts by combining the power of computational capabilities and human intelligence.

sections.text: Beyond static annotation, various interfaces empower users to interact dynamically with ML systems. The Uncertainty-Performance Interface (UPI) couples confidence scores with outcome heat-maps, allowing decision makers to dynamically adjust their thresholds. Research by Bansal et al. indicates that users build more accurate mental models when an AI system discloses its own error likelihood. In the domain of learning from demonstrations (LfD), embedding the process within a configurable user interface empowers users to create customized primitives that the system can execute autonomously, enabling the automation of frequently repeated task sections [6]. Furthermore, some tools allow users to use an API to deliver input and extract output in addition to using a web-based interface, providing flexibility in interaction [5]. question: What is a good Ontology semantic similarity measure that considers multiple inheritance cases of concepts?

sections.title: Addressing Multiple Inheritance in Ontologies
sections.text: A significant challenge in computing semantic similarity within ontological structures is the accurate handling of concepts that possess multiple inheritance paths. Traditional measures often fail to capture the nuanced relationships inherent in such complex hierarchies. To address this limitation, a 2015 study introduced a novel similarity measure specifically designed to account for multiple inheritance in ontologies [2]. This approach aims to provide a more precise assessment of the relationship between concepts by integrating the structural complexity of the ontology into the calculation [2]. Furthermore, a subsequent 2018 paper proposed an improved synthetic weighted algorithm for ontology-based semantic similarity computation, which also targets these structural complexities [1]. The results from this 2018 algorithm indicate that it can effectively solve the problem of multiple inheritance, thereby enhancing the overall accuracy of the similarity computation [1].

sections.title: Incorporating Concept Specificity and Asymmetry
sections.text: Beyond merely tracing inheritance paths, effective similarity measures must also consider the inherent properties of the concepts being evaluated. The 2015 measure explicitly incorporates the common specificity feature of the evaluated concepts to achieve a more accurate similarity score [2]. By factoring in specificity, the measure can better distinguish between general and specific terms, leading to a more granular understanding of their semantic relationship [2]. Additionally, the 2018 improved synthetic weighted algorithm addresses the issue of concept asymmetry, a common problem where the similarity score between two concepts may not be symmetric depending on the direction of comparison [1]. By resolving both the multiple inheritance and asymmetry issues, the 2018 method achieves higher accuracy in its semantic similarity computations compared to previous approaches [1].

sections.title: Evaluation Methodology and Datasets
sections.text: The validity of these proposed measures is established through rigorous evaluation against human expert judgments. The 2015 measure was tested using two distinct datasets consisting of biomedical term pairs that had been scored for similarity by human experts [2]. For these evaluations, the SNOMED CT ontology was utilized as the input ontology, providing a rich and complex domain structure for testing the measure's capabilities [2]. The primary metric for assessment was the correlation between the similarity scores generated by the proposed measure and the human expert scores [2]. This correlation analysis allowed the researchers to quantify how well the automated measure aligned with human perception of semantic similarity [2].

sections.title: Comparative Performance and Accuracy
sections.text: To determine the relative effectiveness of the new measures, they were compared against other existing similarity measures. The 2015 study specifically compared the correlation obtained by its proposed measure with human scores against those of other established measures [2]. This comparative analysis highlights the improvements offered by the new approach in capturing human-like similarity judgments [2]. Similarly, the 2018 paper reports that its improved synthetic weighted algorithm yields results with higher accuracy [1]. This increased accuracy is attributed to the algorithm's ability to handle the specific challenges of multiple inheritance and concept asymmetry [1]. Together, these findings suggest that incorporating structural and specific features of concepts leads to more robust and accurate semantic similarity measures.

question: What is the difference between FMRI datasets and MRI datasets in terms of data analysis?

sections.title: Fundamental Data Structure and Acquisition
sections.text: The primary distinction between fMRI and MRI datasets lies in their dimensional structure and the physiological phenomena they capture. MRI is defined as anatomical imaging that provides high resolution, typically achieving in-plane resolutions of less than 1mm. In contrast, an fMRI dataset is conceptualized as a collection of a large number of data samples situated in a Euclidean space [3]. Structurally, an fMRI dataset can be viewed as a set of cuboid elements, known as voxels, which may have variable dimensions [2]. Each of these voxels is associated with a time-series that contains as many time-points as there are volumes acquired per session [2]. This temporal dimensionality allows fMRI data to capture states related to blood flow, which is considered a superiority over standard MRI data [1]. While MRI focuses on static anatomical structures, fMRI requires the acquisition of multiple volumes over time to construct these time-series, fundamentally altering the data's shape from a static 3D volume to a dynamic 4D structure.

sections.title: Experimental Design and Pre-processing Requirements
sections.text: The analysis of fMRI data is heavily dependent on the experimental design used during acquisition. Unlike standard MRI, fMRI datasets require very detailed designed experiments to be conducted in order to effectively learn about the brain [1]. The first step in fMRI data analysis involves applying a series of pre-processing transformations aimed at correcting for several potential artifacts introduced during data acquisition [2]. These artifacts are a direct consequence of the dynamic nature of the scanning process. In contrast, while MRI images also require processing, the specific need for correcting temporal artifacts and aligning time-series data is unique to the functional modality. The requirement for detailed experimental design means that fMRI data is not merely a snapshot of anatomy but a record of physiological responses to specific stimuli or manipulations, necessitating rigorous pre-processing to ensure the integrity of the time-course data before any statistical analysis can begin.

sections.title: Statistical Analysis and Dimensionality Challenges
sections.text: Conventional statistical analysis of fMRI data aims to determine which specific voxels have a time-course that correlates with a known pattern of stimulation or experimental manipulation [2]. This approach treats the data from one scanning session, comprising t volumes, as a single observation [4]. However, this creates a high-dimensional, low-sample setting, which necessitates the inclusion of restrictions in conventional fMRI analysis approaches to prevent overfitting. To address this, regularization techniques are employed; for instance, L1 and L2 regularization approaches have shown visible improvements over nonconvex alternatives. A new 4D approach to fMRI data analysis has also been presented to handle these complex data structures [4]. The analysis of fMRI signals plays an important role in determining brain activation patterns [3]. For example, the analysis of task-fMRI data during working memory tasks has shown apparent differences in activation. Furthermore, neutrosophic-entropy-based clustering algorithms have been proposed for the analysis of fMRI signals from both working memory tasks and resting-state brain conditions [3]. These methods are critical for extracting meaningful physiological insights from the high-dimensional data.

sections.title: Machine Learning and Representation Learning
sections.text: Machine learning techniques are increasingly applied to fMRI data to uncover complex patterns. A study comparing machine learning classifiers utilized fMRI data from the Haxby dataset [1]. In the domain of natural language processing and brain decoding, fMRI data from word observation tasks has been connected with shallow embeddings such as GloVe and Word2Vec. This integration allows for the mapping of linguistic features to neural activity. The use of specific datasets like the Haxby dataset highlights the importance of standardized benchmarks in evaluating the performance of these classifiers. The ability to link fMRI time-series with external representations, such as word embeddings, demonstrates the versatility of fMRI data in bridging cognitive science and computational modeling. These approaches move beyond simple correlation with stimulation patterns to more complex representations of brain function.

sections.title: MRI-Specific Analysis: Style Transfer and Reconstruction
sections.text: In contrast to the time-series focus of fMRI, MRI analysis often deals with spatial consistency and reconstruction. A novel medical image style transfer method called StyleMapper has been introduced to transfer medical scans to an unseen style using limited training data [5]. This method is particularly effective for MRI, as it allows for the alignment of medical images taken with different scanners into a single unified style dataset [5]. This alignment is crucial for training downstream tasks such as classification and detection [5]. Experimental results on breast magnetic resonance images have indicated the effectiveness of this style transfer method [5]. Additionally, SwinMR, a Swin transformer-based model, has been developed for fast MRI reconstruction. These techniques address the variability in MRI data arising from different hardware and acquisition protocols, ensuring that anatomical features are consistent across datasets. This is distinct from fMRI analysis, which prioritizes the temporal dynamics of blood flow over the spatial consistency of anatomical structures.

sections.title: Clinical Applications and Multi-Modal Integration
sections.text: Spatial prediction plays a critical role in automatic medical diagnosis from MRI imagery, including monitoring infectious disease, mapping disease risk, and detecting disease outbreaks [8]. Medical image databases often include images from various sources such as CT, X-ray, MRI, and PET, covering different body parts like the brain, lung, and abdomen [7]. In clinical settings, segmentation labels derived from MRI scans serve as ground truth for evaluating diagnostic algorithms. Multi-modal approaches are also common; for instance, an attention-like mechanism has been illustrated where multi-modal MRI at the reference time point is multiplied with subtraction images, which act as the attention gate [6]. The APIS dataset, designed as a paired CT-MRI dataset for ischemic stroke, exemplifies the integration of different imaging modalities. In such clinical studies, a high percentage of patients, specifically 98.8%, had additional MRI modalities such as T1 provided, along with DWI images, B0, and ADC maps. This multi-modal richness is a key feature of clinical MRI datasets, whereas fMRI datasets are typically focused on the temporal evolution of a single functional signal.
